## The result in brief {.smaller}

![](assets/rpt-energy.svg){.fig-wide}

::: kpis
::: {.kpi .blue}
[41% less]{.big}
[energy lost by the proposed LP-ESC than by the best published design, the LP-ESC of Ciri, Leonardi & Rotea 2019 (same one-day tracking time): 0.385% → 0.227%, about 27 MWh per turbine-year at 8 m/s]{.lab}
:::
::: {.kpi .gold}
[12× less]{.big}
[by the proposed LP-PIESC than by the LP-PIESC of Kumar & Rotea 2022, same estimator: 3.19% → 0.275%, about 500 MWh per turbine-year]{.lab}
:::
::: {.kpi .hot}
[46% less]{.big}
[by the proposed LP-ESC than by the LP-ESC tuning of Kumar & Rotea 2022, both tracking the optimum in 740 s: 4.51% → 2.42%, about 360 MWh per turbine-year]{.lab}
:::
:::

[Six-day simulations of the nonlinear NREL 5 MW turbine at 8 m/s, turbulence intensity 0.10, four wind records per spectrum; every controller runs in the same wind as a turbine held at the optimum. Each published design is paired with the proposed design of the same type, tracking at least as fast. Bars: mean over records, lines: range. Solid: Kaimal; light: von Kármán.]{.tiny}

::: notes
The headline. The proposed design, an ordinary demodulation loop tuned from the turbulence
spectrum, loses 0.23 percent of the energy. The best published design, also demodulation
and at the same one-day tracking time, loses 0.39. Each comparison is like for like: same
controller type, same or slower tracking. The 2022 demodulation tuning tracks in 740
seconds and loses 4.5 percent; the proposed design for 740 seconds loses 2.4. The 2022
least-squares LP-PIESC tracks in 5.1 days and loses 3.2 percent; the same estimator with
the proposed tuning tracks in one day and loses 0.275. The rest of the talk is where these
numbers come from, and why the prediction and the simulation agree.
:::

## One gain, unknown and drifting {.smaller}

::: cols2w
::: {}
![](assets/regions.svg)

Below rated wind speed the turbine should run at the tip-speed ratio $\lambda = R\Omega/V$
that maximizes the power coefficient $C_P(\lambda)$. The standard controller sets the generator
torque to $u\,\Omega^2$; the **gain** $u$ alone fixes where the rotor settles, at every wind
speed (Unit 1).
:::
::: {}
![](assets/cp-curve.svg)

The best gain $u^\star$ depends on the blades, which erode, ice and foul. It must be
**found online**, and found again when it moves.
:::
:::

::: notes
At a fixed tip-speed ratio, both torques scale as V squared, so the wind cancels and
the gain alone sets lambda. The optimum is one number, but it drifts with the blades.
:::

## Extremum seeking finds it, by two routes {.smaller}

![](assets/esc-loop.svg){.fig-band}

1. **Dither**: add $a\sin\omega t$ to the gain, period $T = 2\pi/\omega$.
2. **Estimate**: read from log-power $y = \ln P$ how power changes with the gain.
3. **Step**: move the gain uphill, once per period (step size $\kappa$) or continuously.

::: cols2
::: card
[LP-ESC: demodulation]{.cardh}
Correlate $y$ with the dither over each period: the **in-phase channel** $\hat g$ [Rotea 2017; Ciri, Leonardi & Rotea 2019].
:::
::: card
[LP-PIESC: least squares]{.cardh}
Fit $\dot y \approx \theta_0 + \theta_1(\nu - \hat\nu)$ by recursive least squares; proportional-integral update [Kumar & Rotea 2022]. Here $\nu = \nu^\star u/u^\star$ is the normalized gain ($\nu^\star = 0.061$) and $\hat\nu$ the integrator state, about which the dither swings.
:::
:::

::: notes
Both are log-power schemes: the log removes the mean wind speed from the loop gain.
They differ in how they turn the response into a gradient.
:::

## LP-PIESC: a least-squares fit in place of the correlation {.smaller}

![](assets/rpt-piesc-loop.svg){.fig-band}

Published tuning [Kumar & Rotea 2022]: $T = 314$ s, $a = 0.082\,\nu^\star$, estimator memory
$1/k_T = 0.05$ s, ridge $q = 10^{-6}$, $k_p = 5\times10^{-6}$ s, $\tau_I = 2.8$. Reported to reach the optimum almost at once, with a quarter of
the classical dither.

::: notes
Keep in mind two numbers: a memory of a twentieth of a second, and a period of five
minutes. Their ratio is what decides what this estimator reads.
:::

## Turbulence makes the gain scatter {.smaller}

![](assets/rpt-wander.svg){.fig-wide}

::: claim
**Scatter** $\sigma(\tilde u)$: the standard deviation of the gain error $\tilde u = u - u^\star$
once the loop has settled, a spread over time quoted as a fraction of $u^\star$. It concerns
the center of the dither only; the dither's own cost is counted separately. Every
excursion costs power. With $J(u)$ the log-power at rest at gain $u$ (apart from a constant set by
the wind), which peaks at $u^\star$, the loss is $\tfrac12|J''|\,\sigma(\tilde u)^2$ plus the dither's cost.
:::

::: notes
Left: the 2022 LP-PIESC in four wind records over six days, started at the optimum. It
random-walks. Right: the same LP-PIESC estimator with the proposed design (60 s period,
amplitude 0.111, one-day tracking time), same winds. The scatter is the size of this motion.
:::

## What this work answers

Given the wind's spectral density and the tuning of each controller:

1. How noisy is **one gradient estimate** at the optimum, and what does LP-PIESC's estimate measure?
2. How large is the **scatter** of the gain in steady state?
3. How much **power is lost**, and which tuning loses least for a required tracking time?
4. How do **LP-ESC and LP-PIESC** compare, and do the predictions survive **simulation**, including the published runs?

::: claim
**The answer in one line.** Write the wind speed as $V = \bar V(1+\varepsilon)$, with mean
$\bar V$ and relative fluctuation $\varepsilon$. At the optimum the wind enters log-power as $3\varepsilon$, so
each estimate is the wind seen through a known window; a slow loop (one whose tracking time spans many dither periods) sees only the wind's
density at the dither frequency; the scatter, the loss and the best tuning then follow
in closed form from **three numbers**: that density, the curvature of $C_P$ at its peak,
and the rotor time constant.
:::

::: notes
Everything that follows is this one sentence, unpacked and checked.
:::

## The argument in one line

![](assets/rpt-chain.svg)

::: cols3
::: card
[The wind]{.cardh}
$\Phi(f_1)$: the turbulence density at the dither frequency $f_1 = 1/T$ (IEC Kaimal or von Kármán).
:::
::: card
[The rotor]{.cardh}
$\tau_r = 6.88$ s: the time constant with which the rotor follows the gain (at 8 m/s).
:::
::: card
[The power curve]{.cardh}
$\chi = 6.3$: how sharply $C_P$ peaks; $|J''(u^\star)|\,u^{\star2} = \chi/9 = 0.70$.
:::
:::

::: notes
Five links, each checked in simulation. Then the design, and the evidence on energy.
:::

## Link 1: at the optimum, the wind enters log-power as $3\varepsilon$ {.smaller}

::: cols2w
::: {}
![](assets/rpt-logpower.svg)
:::
::: {}
With $V = \bar V(1 + \varepsilon)$, power is $\propto V^3 C_P(\lambda)$, so
$$y = \ln P = \text{const} + 3\ln(1+\varepsilon) + \ln C_P(\lambda).$$

At $u^\star$ the power curve is **flat**: $C_P'(\lambda^\star) = 0$, so the wind's effect through
$\lambda$ drops out at first order, and
$$y - \mathbb{E}[y] = 3\,\varepsilon + O(\sigma_\varepsilon^2),$$
where $\sigma_\varepsilon$, the standard deviation of $\varepsilon$, is the turbulence intensity (0.10).

[Simulation: slope 3.086 (Kaimal), 3.090 (von Kármán); correlation 0.991.]{.small}
:::
:::

::: notes
A gust changes power only through the cube of the wind speed, because at the peak the
power curve is flat. That single term makes everything else linear.
:::

## Link 2: one estimate sees the spectrum through a window {.smaller}

![](assets/rpt-window.svg){.fig-band}

The demodulated estimate correlates $y$ with $\sin\omega t$, so its noise is
$6Z_n/(aT)$ with $Z_n = \int_0^T \varepsilon(nT+t)\sin\omega t\,dt$, and
$$\operatorname{Var}(Z) = \int \Phi(f)\,|\hat w(f)|^2\,df ,$$
where $\hat w(f) = \int_0^T \sin(\omega t)\,e^{-i2\pi ft}\,dt$, the dither's Fourier transform over one period, is the estimate's window on the wind.

[Both windows pass $f_1$ equally; the sine window leans to low frequencies, where the wind has its energy, so the quadrature (cosine) channel is the quieter one per estimate (Units 12–14).]{.small}

::: notes
A linear filter of a stationary wind: its variance is the spectrum integrated against
the filter's squared gain.
:::

## Checked over a tenfold range of dither periods {.smaller}

![](assets/rpt-noise-period.svg){.fig-wide}

::: claim
Predicted and simulated standard deviation of one estimate agree within **0.5 – 2.2 %**
for $T$ from 60 to 600 s under both spectra, with **no fitted parameter**; the small excess
is the size and sign of the terms the prediction leaves out.
:::

::: notes
240 periods per point; sampling uncertainty about 4.6 percent per point.
:::

## The two IEC turbulence spectra {.smaller}

::: cols2w
::: {}
![](assets/rpt-spectra.svg)
:::
::: {}
- Same flat level $4\sigma_\varepsilon^2 L/\bar V$, so $L$ is the integral length scale:
  **340 m** (Kaimal), **147 m** (von Kármán) at the 90 m hub.
- Both fall as $f^{-5/3}$; they differ mainly near their corners.
- At the published period (314 s) the densities agree within **3 %**; at 60, 150, 600 s
  their ratio is 0.79, 0.81, 1.35.
- Effect on the predicted scatter: at most **11 %** over 60–314 s. **No conclusion changes.**
:::
:::

::: notes
Everything is worked out twice, on equal footing. The spectrum enters only through its
value at the dither frequency.
:::

## Link 3: the published LP-PIESC reads the quadrature channel {.smaller}

::: cols2w
::: {}
![](assets/rpt-channels.svg)
:::
::: {}
The regressor is $[1, d]$, with $d = \nu - \hat\nu = a\sin\omega t$ the dither (proportional
term neglected). Over a 0.05 s memory it is frozen, so the ridge fit, with effective ridge
weight $\gamma = 4\times10^{-4}$, returns the minimum-norm product
$$\hat\theta_1 = \frac{d\,\dot y}{1 + d^2 + \gamma},$$
whose period average is the **cosine** (quadrature) coefficient of $y$. The rotor returns
the dither in phase with gain $G_1 = 1/(1+(\omega\tau_r)^2)$, which demodulation reads, and a
quarter period late with gain $G_q = \omega\tau_r G_1$, which this estimate reads:
**0.135** against **0.981** at 314 s.

[Simulation: $\hat\theta_1$ follows $d\,\dot y$ with correlation 0.997; in-phase / quadrature 7.24, predicted $1/(\omega\tau_r) = 7.27$.]{.small}
:::
:::

::: notes
The estimator sees the gradient only through the rotor's lag. A rotor without lag would
give it no gradient signal at all.
:::

## Link 4: a slow loop sees one frequency {.smaller}

::: cols2w
::: {}
![](assets/rpt-loop.svg)
:::
::: {}
Each period a loop corrects a fraction $K = T/\tau_c$ of the gain error; it is **slow** when
${K \ll 1}$ (one day at 60 s: ${K = 7\times10^{-4}}$). Averaging $N$ estimates is one estimate over
$N$ periods; its window narrows onto $f_1$ (Fejér). So the noise a slow loop feels is the **long-run variance**
$$\sigma_\infty^2 = \frac{2\Psi}{a^2T},\qquad \Psi = 9\,\Phi(f_1),$$
and the scatter at tracking time $\tau_c$ is
$$\sigma(\tilde u)^2 = \frac{\Psi}{a^2 g^2\,\tau_c\,J''^2},\quad g = G_1 \text{ or } G_q .$$

[Simulated loops: within **4 %** of the long-run prediction; one period's variance overstates by up to 18 %.]{.small}
:::
:::

::: notes
The period cancels from the scatter once you fix the tracking time; the wind enters
through its density at one frequency.
:::

## Link 5: loss = scatter + dither; the best amplitude balances them {.smaller}

::: cols2w
::: {}
![](assets/rpt-loss-amplitude.svg)
:::
::: {}
$$\ell(a) = \underbrace{\frac{\Psi}{2a^2g^2\tau_c|J''|}}_{\text{scatter}} + \underbrace{\frac{|J''|G_1a^2}{4\vphantom{2a^2g^2\tau_c|J''|}}}_{\text{dither}}$$

Least when the two are **equal**:
$$a_{\mathrm{opt}} = \Big(\frac{2\Psi}{g^2G_1\tau_cJ''^2}\Big)^{1/4},\qquad
\ell_{\mathrm{min}} = \sqrt{\frac{\Psi G_1}{2\tau_c g^2}}.$$

The step size or integral time then follows from the tracking time:
$$\begin{aligned}\kappa &= \frac{T}{\tau_cG_1|J''|} &&\text{(LP-ESC)},\\[2pt] \tau_I &= \frac{\tau_c\pi a^2G_q|J''|}{T} &&\text{(LP-PIESC)}.\end{aligned}$$
:::
:::

::: notes
A larger dither lets a loop of fixed tracking time take smaller steps and scatter less,
but the dither itself costs power. The least loss balances the two.
:::

## Choosing the period {.smaller}

![](assets/rpt-design.svg){.fig-wide}

::: claim
Shorter periods move $f_1$ up the falling spectrum, so the least loss falls, until the
rotor's lag takes over. **Recommendation: $T = 60$ s** (about nine rotor time constants):
LP-ESC **0.21 %**, LP-PIESC **0.29 %** (Kaimal, one day), against 0.41 % and 2.98 % at 314 s.
The quadrature penalty $1/(\omega\tau_r)$ falls from **7.3** to **1.4**.
:::

::: notes
Below about 45 seconds the static power curve and the first-order rotor are least
reliable, so we stop at 60.
:::

## The published LP-PIESC tracks in 5.1 days {.smaller}

![](assets/rpt-reproduce.svg){.fig-wide}

::: claim
Its integral path is a slow loop on the quadrature channel with loop gain
$7.13\times10^{-4}$ per period: tracking time **5.1 days**, stationary scatter **0.33 $u^\star$**,
loss **3.9 %** (Kaimal). The published fast convergence appears only when the integrator
**starts at the optimum**, which the closed-form optimum makes possible.
:::

::: notes
LP-ESC with its published tuning converges in about 1000 seconds, as reported. LP-PIESC
barely moves from any other start in 3000 seconds.
:::

![](assets/rpt-tracking.svg){.fig-wide}

Gain started at **0.8 $u^\star$**. Energy lost on the first day: proposed LP-ESC **0.67 %**

## Gains over the published designs

::: kpis
::: {.kpi .blue}
[−41 %]{.big}
[proposed LP-ESC vs. the best published design (LP-ESC, Ciri, Leonardi & Rotea 2019, same tracking time): 0.16 points, **27 MWh** per turbine-year at 8 m/s. Von Kármán: −36 %.]{.lab}
:::
::: {.kpi .gold}
[÷12]{.big}
[proposed LP-PIESC vs. LP-PIESC, Kumar & Rotea 2022, same estimator: 3.19 % → 0.275 %, 2.92 points, **499 MWh** per turbine-year. Von Kármán: ÷10.]{.lab}
:::
::: {.kpi .hot}
[−46 %]{.big}
[proposed LP-ESC vs. LP-ESC, Kumar & Rotea 2022, same tracking time (740 s): 4.51 % → 2.42 %, 2.09 points, **358 MWh** per turbine-year. Von Kármán: −40 %.]{.lab}
:::
:::

::: remark
Measured in our simulator: NREL 5 MW rotor with a static power curve and a first-order
rotor, aerodynamic power, 8 m/s, turbulence intensity 0.10, synthesized turbulence. The
published designs were tuned in other simulators; the comparison holds turbine, wind and
tracking time fixed for both LP-ESC comparisons, so the design is the only difference; the proposed LP-PIESC tracks five times faster than the published one. Reference
turbine: 1.95 MW mean, 17.1 GWh per year at this wind.
:::

::: notes
The gain over the best published design comes entirely from the period and the
amplitude: shorter period, amplitude set where scatter and dither cost the same. Against
the 2022 LP-ESC the amplitude is almost the same (0.31 against 0.33); the gain is the
period. At 60 seconds the rotor passes less of the dither, so the dither costs 1.1 percent
rather than 1.9, and the wind's density at the dither frequency is lower. A 740-second
tracking time is expensive: at one day the same rules lose 0.23 percent.
:::

## When is LP-PIESC the right choice?

::: cols2
::: card
[The gap is a tuning choice]{.cardh}
The penalty comes from the 0.05 s memory plus fitting $\dot y$. Fit $y$ itself over a full
period and least squares reads the **in-phase** channel, with demodulation's loss. At
60 s the published estimator costs only **20 %** more (0.275 vs 0.227 %).
:::
::: card
[Least squares gives more than an estimate]{.cardh}
An explicit model, an information matrix that can serve as an **error bar**, and updates
in **continuous time**: useful for a loop that acts on its own uncertainty.
:::
::: card
[The quadrature channel's one merit]{.cardh}
A slow wind **drift** within a period reads as gradient in the sine window but cancels in
the cosine window. It loses more signal ($\times\omega\tau_r$) than it saves in noise.
:::
::: card
[Speed was the published motivation]{.cardh}
This work measures steady-state loss of a slow loop and neglects the proportional path.
Whether a retuned least-squares loop **recovers faster** after the optimum moves is open.
:::
:::

::: notes
For steady-state energy capture, choose demodulation or a full-period least-squares fit.
Choose LP-PIESC's structure where its model, its error bar or a faster transient is
needed, and tune it by these rules.
:::

## The design procedure {.bk}

::: cols2
::: {}
**Three numbers**

1. $\tau_r = \dfrac{2I\lambda^{\star2}}{3\rho\pi R^4\bar V C_P^{\mathrm{max}}}$ from the rotor data.
2. $\chi$ from the design power curve: ${|J''(u^\star)| = \chi/(9u^{\star2})}$.
3. ${\Psi = 9\,\Phi(1/T)}$ from the site's spectrum (or the IEC model).

**One choice**: the tracking time $\tau_c$ (blades change over weeks; recover from
start-up within a day: ${\tau_c = 1}$ day).
:::
::: {}
**Then**

4. $T \approx 9\,\tau_r$ (60 s here).
5. $a = a_{\mathrm{opt}}$.
6. ${\kappa = T/(\tau_cG_1|J''|)}$ or ${\tau_I = \tau_c\pi a^2G_q|J''|/T}$.

::: claim
A design curvature ${J''_\mathrm{d} = rJ''}$ leaves the loop unbiased, scales the tracking time
by $r$, and costs ${(\sqrt r + 1/\sqrt r)/2}$ of the least loss for that tracking time: 6 % at
$r = 2$ (B15).
:::
:::
:::

::: notes
Everything needed before any simulation is run.
:::

## Limits, and the next step {.bk}

- **The design needs $J''$.** It comes from the design power curve, and the true curvature
  drifts with the blades, as $u^\star$ does. A design curvature ${J''_\mathrm{d} = rJ''}$
  leaves the loop unbiased, scales its tracking time by $r$, and costs
  ${(\sqrt r + 1/\sqrt r)/2}$ of the least loss for that tracking time: measured **+5 %** at
  $r = \tfrac12$ and **+8 %** at $r = 2$ (B15). The design also needs $\Phi(f_1)$ at the site,
  and $\tau_r$, which varies as $1/\bar V$.
- **The wind model**: stationary, with fixed mean speed and turbulence intensity, while a day
  mixes wind states; point spectra, while the rotor averages the wind over its disk.
- **The turbine model**: static power curve and first-order rotor; aerodynamic, not electrical,
  power (the term $I\Omega\dot\Omega$ matters when $\omega\tau_r$ is not small: 0.72 at 60 s).
- **The simulations use the same spectra** as the analysis: they test the derivation, not the wind models.
- **LP-PIESC**: its proportional path $k_p\hat\theta_1$, the term that adds the current
  estimate to the gain, moves the gain ${4.5\times10^{-8}}$ as much as the integral path per
  period at the published $k_p$. A $k_p$ raised for speed, and the projection, are not analyzed.

::: openq
**Next:** measure $J''$ online; test on measured turbine data and electrical power; measure
recovery after the optimum moves, where LP-PIESC's proportional path was meant to act.
:::

## Summary

::: claim
1. At the optimum the wind enters log-power as **$3\varepsilon$**, so each gradient estimate is the wind seen through a known window.
2. A slow loop sees only the wind's density **at the dither frequency**; the scatter is $\sqrt{\Psi/(a^2g^2\tau_cJ''^2)}$.
3. The published LP-PIESC reads the **quadrature channel**, $\omega\tau_r$ of the signal, and tracks in **5.1 days**.
4. Loss = scatter + dither; the **minimum-loss design** follows from three numbers, at $T \approx 9\tau_r$.
5. Measured over six days: **0.23 %** lost, **41 % less** than the best published design; **46 % less** than the 2022 LP-ESC tuning at its 740 s tracking time; the same rules cut the 2022 LP-PIESC's loss **12×** while tracking five times faster.
:::

## B1: The rest point, and why the wind cancels {#b1 .bk}

At a fixed tip-speed ratio $\lambda = R\Omega/V$, both torques on the rotor scale as $V^2$:

::: cols2
::: card
[Aerodynamic torque]{.cardh}
$$\tfrac12\rho\pi R^3V^2\,\frac{C_P(\lambda)}{\lambda}$$
:::
::: card
[Generator torque]{.cardh}
$$u\,\Omega^2 = u\,\frac{\lambda^2V^2}{R^2}$$
:::
:::

so their balance is free of the wind:

::: eqbox
$$\frac{C_P(\lambda)}{\lambda^3} = c_u\,u,\qquad c_u = \frac{2}{\rho\pi R^5}.$$
:::

::: cols2
::: card
[One stable rest point]{.cardh}
For every gain below $1.86\,u^\star$ there is exactly one, $\lambda_{\mathrm{eq}}(u)$, on the branch through
$\lambda^\star$; near it the rotor is first order with time constant $\tau_r$ (Units 1–2).
:::
::: card
[The objective]{.cardh}
Log-power at rest is a wind constant plus $J(u) = \ln C_P(\lambda_{\mathrm{eq}}(u))$, which peaks at
$u^\star = 2.23\times10^6$ N m s² with $J''(u^\star) = -\chi/(9u^{\star2})$ (Unit 3).
:::
:::

## B2: The rotor time constant, and the inertia {#b2 .bk}

::: eqbox
$$\tau_r = \frac{2I\lambda^{\star2}}{3\rho\pi R^4\bar V C_P^{\mathrm{max}}} = 6.88\ \text{s at } 8\ \text{m/s},\qquad \tau_r\propto 1/\bar V.$$
:::

The rotor's inertia $I_{\mathrm{rotor}}$ follows from the NREL 5 MW blade and hub data, moving each blade
to the shaft by the parallel-axis theorem:
$$I_{\mathrm{rotor}} = 3\cos^2\beta_p\,(I_b + 2r_hS_b + m_br_h^2) + 115\,926\ \text{kg m}^2,$$

[with $\beta_p$ the precone angle, $r_h$ the hub radius, $m_b$, $S_b$, $I_b$ the blade's mass and its first and second mass moments about its root, and 115 926 kg m² the hub.]{.small}

::: stats
::: stat
[3.88 × 10⁷ kg m²]{.num}
[the rotor, $I_{\mathrm{rotor}}$]{.lab}
:::
::: stat
[+ 97² × 534 kg m²]{.num}
[the generator, seen through the 97 : 1 gearbox]{.lab}
:::
::: stat
[4.38 × 10⁷ kg m²]{.num}
[the total, $I$]{.lab}
:::
:::

::: remark
[Kumar & Rotea 2022] use $3.54\times10^7$ kg m², which omits the hub-radius offset $r_h = 1.5$ m.
:::

## B3: The rotor seen from the gain {#b3 .bk}

From the gain to log-power, the rotor is a first-order lag with unit static gain and time
constant $\tau_r$, followed by the slope $J'$. A dither $a\sin\omega t$ therefore returns as

::: eqbox
$$\delta y = J'a\,(G_1\sin\omega t - G_q\cos\omega t),\qquad G_1 = \frac{1}{1+(\omega\tau_r)^2},\quad G_q = \omega\tau_rG_1 .$$
:::

::: stats
::: stat
[0.981 / 0.135]{.num}
[$G_1$ / $G_q$ at the published period, $T$ = 314 s]{.lab}
:::
::: stat
[0.66 / 0.48]{.num}
[$G_1$ / $G_q$ at the recommended period, $T$ = 60 s]{.lab}
:::
::: {.stat .gold}
[43 s]{.num}
[$T = 2\pi\tau_r$: the two cross, and $G_q = 1/2$ is largest (Unit 4)]{.lab}
:::
:::

::: claim
Demodulation reads the in-phase part $G_1$; the published LP-PIESC estimator reads the
quadrature part $G_q$ (Link 3).
:::

## B4: The estimate in calm wind {#b4 .bk}

::: cols2
::: card
[A Fourier coefficient]{.cardh}
$$\hat g_n = B_1/a,\qquad \hat g^c_n = A_1/a,$$
with $B_1$ and $A_1$ the first sine and cosine coefficients of $y$ over period $n$. It ignores
the mean and every higher harmonic, but a drift within the period reads as gradient (Unit 5).
:::
::: card
[Its bias]{.cardh}
$$\hat g_n = J'(u_n) + \tfrac{a^2}{8}J'''(u_n) + O(a^4),$$
with $u_n$ the center of the dither in period $n$ (Unit 6).
:::
:::

At $a = 0.136\,u^\star$:

::: stats
::: stat
[0.37 %]{.num}
[above $u^\star$: where the bias makes the loop settle]{.lab}
:::
::: stat
[5 × 10⁻⁶]{.num}
[of the power: what that offset costs]{.lab}
:::
::: {.stat .gold}
[0.32 %]{.num}
[of the power: what the dither itself costs]{.lab}
:::
:::

::: claim
The bias is negligible. The error that matters is random.
:::

## B5: The wind as a random process {#b5 .bk}

::: cols2
::: card
[The model]{.cardh}
$$V = \bar V(1+\varepsilon),\qquad \Gamma(\tau) = \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon(t)\varepsilon(t+\tau)],$$
with $\varepsilon$ stationary and $|\Gamma| \le \Gamma(0) = \sigma_\varepsilon^2 = \mathrm{TI}^2$.
:::
::: card
[Its spectrum]{.cardh}
$$\Phi(f) = \int\Gamma(\tau)e^{-i2\pi f\tau}d\tau,\qquad \sigma_\varepsilon^2 = \int_0^\infty S\,df,$$
with $S = 2\Phi$ the one-sided density (Units 7–8).
:::
::: card
[Orders of smallness]{.cardh}
Remainders are ranked by RMS in powers of $\sigma_\varepsilon$. With sixth moments finite,
products of $k \le 3$ filtered winds are $O(\sigma_\varepsilon^k)$ (Unit 9).
:::
::: card
[What the tip-speed ratio sees]{.cardh}
The **high-passed** wind, with corner $1/(2\pi\tau_r) = 0.023$ Hz; the mean of $\lambda$ stays at
$\lambda^\star$ to second order (Unit 10).
:::
:::

::: stats
::: stat
[72 %]{.num}
[of the Kaimal variance lies below that corner, where the rotor follows the wind]{.lab}
:::
:::

## B6: The least-squares estimator, unpacked {#b6 .bk}

::: cols3
::: card
[1 · A weighted ridge fit]{.cardh}
At every instant the recursion returns the minimizer of an exponentially weighted ridge cost
with memory $1/k_T = 0.05$ s (Unit 15).
:::
::: card
[2 · A fit of filtered $\dot y$]{.cardh}
With $\tilde y$ the prediction error and $c$ the filtered regressor, the states combine into
$$z = \tilde y + c^\top\hat\theta,\quad \dot z = -k_fz + \dot y.$$
So the estimator regresses $\dot y$, low-passed at rate $k_f$, on the equally filtered
regressor (Unit 16).
:::
::: card
[3 · A frozen regressor]{.cardh}
Over the memory the regressor barely moves, so the fit is the **minimum-norm** product,
whose period average is the quadrature channel (Unit 17).
:::
:::

::: stats
::: stat
[γ = 4 × 10⁻⁴]{.num}
[effective ridge weight, $qk_f^2$]{.lab}
:::
::: stat
[𝓜 = 0.0025]{.num}
[memory number $\omega^2/(k_T^2\gamma)$: small means frozen]{.lab}
:::
:::

::: claim
A fit of $y$ itself on $[1, d]$ over a full period returns the in-phase channel instead.
:::

## B7: Correlated noise and the long-run variance {#b7 .bk}

A first-order recursion $x_{n+1} = \alpha x_n + \kappa v_n$, driven by noise $v_n$ of variance
$\sigma_v^2$ and correlation $\rho_k$ between values $k$ steps apart, has variance

::: eqbox
$$\operatorname{Var}(x) = \frac{\kappa^2\sigma_v^2}{1-\alpha^2}\Big[1 + 2\sum_{k\ge1}\alpha^k\rho_k\Big].$$
:::

::: cols2
::: card
[A slow loop, $\alpha \to 1$]{.cardh}
The bracket tends to $1 + 2\sum_{k\ge1}\rho_k$, and $\sigma_\infty^2 = \sigma_v^2\big(1 + 2\sum_{k\ge1}\rho_k\big)$
is the **long-run variance** of the noise (Units 20–21).
:::
::: card
[In the frequency domain]{.cardh}
Summed with Fejér's kernel, $\sigma_\infty^2 = 2\Psi/(a^2T)$, for both channels (Unit 22).
:::
:::

::: stats
::: {.stat .gold}
[1.29 ×]{.num}
[one period's variance against the long-run value, in-phase channel (Kaimal, $T$ = 150 s)]{.lab}
:::
::: stat
[0.87 ×]{.num}
[the same ratio for the quadrature channel]{.lab}
:::
:::

## B8: Short records under-measure the scatter {#b8 .bk}

The sample variance $s^2$ of a record falls short of the true variance $\sigma^2$ by the variance
of the record's own mean $\bar x$ (Unit 21):

::: eqbox
$$\mathbb{E}[s^2] = \sigma^2 - \operatorname{Var}(\bar x).$$
:::

::: stats
::: stat
[2 days]{.num}
[record length]{.lab}
:::
::: stat
[6 h]{.num}
[tracking time of the loop: the record spans eight tracking times]{.lab}
:::
::: {.stat .hot}
[0.88]{.num}
[sample standard deviation over true: a 12 % shortfall]{.lab}
:::
:::

::: claim
The nonlinear comparison of LP-PIESC against demodulation applies this factor to its predictions.
:::

## B9: Away from the optimum {#b9 .bk}

Away from $u^\star$ the rotor adds a high-passed copy of the wind to log-power, with weight
$\eta$, the slope of $\ln C_P$ against $\ln\lambda$ at the mean tip-speed ratio. The standard
deviation of the noise is multiplied by $|1 + \eta H(f_1)/3|$, where

::: eqbox
$$\eta \approx 2.1\,\frac{\tilde u}{u^\star},\qquad H(f) = \frac{-i2\pi f\tau_r}{1+i2\pi f\tau_r}\ \ \text{(the rotor's high-pass)}.$$
:::

::: stats
::: stat
[0.1 $u^\star$]{.num}
[scatter of a converged loop]{.lab}
:::
::: stat
[≈ 2 %]{.num}
[change in the noise at that scatter (Unit 26)]{.lab}
:::
:::

::: claim
The noise model derived at $u^\star$ holds over the gains a converged loop visits.
:::

## B10: The synthesized wind {#b10 .bk}

A sum of cosines with independent uniform phases $\Theta_k$:

::: eqbox
$$\varepsilon(t) = \sum_{k=1}^{M} A_k\cos(2\pi f_kt + \Theta_k),\qquad f_k = \frac{k}{D},\quad A_k = \sqrt{2S(f_k)/D},$$
:::

with $D$ the record length and $f_M = 1/(2\Delta t)$ the Nyquist frequency of the sampling
interval $\Delta t$. The sum is strictly stationary, with the target spectrum on its frequency grid (Unit 27).

::: stats
::: {.stat .hot}
[2.7 %]{.num}
[of the variance missing from a ten-hour record at $\Delta t$ = 0.5 s, mostly above the Nyquist frequency]{.lab}
:::
::: stat
[9.86 %]{.num}
[so its turbulence intensity (Kaimal; target 10 %)]{.lab}
:::
::: stat
[−0.002]{.num}
[excess kurtosis: Gaussian]{.lab}
:::
:::

::: claim
Runs under the two spectra share their random phases.
:::

## B11: Where the optimum sits in turbulence {#b11 .smaller}

![](assets/rpt-optimum.svg){.fig-band}

Fixed gains, no dither: the energy peaks at **0.99 $u^\star$**; mean log-power, which the loops
climb, at **1.013 $u^\star$** (1.014 von Kármán). The difference costs about 0.02 % of the energy.
The dither alone, center held at $u^\star$, costs **exactly** the calm-wind $\tfrac14|J''|G_1a^2$:
0.102 % at 60 s and 0.094 $u^\star$, 0.116 % for the published LP-PIESC dither.

## B12: Why the 2022 LP-ESC tuning loses 4.5 % {#b12 .bk}

::: cols2
::: card
[Its dither]{.cardh}
$a = 0.33\,u^\star$ at $T$ = 314 s costs **1.94 %** on its own (measured; the quadratic formula
gives 1.88 %).
:::
::: card
[Its integrator]{.cardh}
Fast: it reaches the optimum's neighborhood within the first hour, but swings the gain by
**0.17 $u^\star$** root-mean-square, about a mean 10 % above $u^\star$.
:::
:::

::: stats
::: {.stat .hot}
[4.5 %]{.num}
[lost in all, steady, independent of the start]{.lab}
:::
::: {.stat .gold}

[its tracking time, from the linearized loop]{.lab}
:::
::: stat
[2.42 %]{.num}
[lost by the proposed LP-ESC for the same 740 s ($T$ = 60 s, $a$ = 0.31 $u^\star$); predicted 2.22 %]{.lab}

[Linearized loop of the 2022 tuning: high-pass 0.018 s⁻¹, demodulation phase 0.36 rad, integrator gain 0.001.]{.small}

Same amplitude, shorter period: the proposed design's dither costs 1.11 % instead of 1.88 %.

## B13: Simulation setup {#b13 .smaller}

::: {.bigtable .kv}
| | |
|---|---|
| turbine | NREL 5 MW rotor, Heier power curve rescaled to $(7.48, 0.4895)$, $I = 4.38\times10^7$ kg m² |
| wind | 8 m/s, TI 0.10, Kaimal ($L$ = 340 m) and von Kármán (147 m), synthesized, 0.5 s |
| integration | adaptive Runge–Kutta (open-loop tests of one estimate); explicit Euler, 5 ms (every closed loop, both controllers) |
| energy runs | six controllers + reference at $u^\star$, same wind; 6 days × 4 records × 2 spectra × 2 starts |
| left out | pitch, power limit, generator and converter dynamics, drivetrain flexibility; one wind speed acts on the whole rotor |
| constants | $u^\star$ by Newton on $J'$, $J''$ by automatic differentiation: $|J''|u^{\star2} = 0.7017$ (designs use $0.7022 = 6.32/9$); $\tau_r$ = 6.878 s |
| checks | 629 stated numbers recomputed from formulas and stored results by the claim checker |
:::

[Every run is specified in full (equations as implemented, initial states, seeds, record lengths, statistics) in Appendix D of the technical report.]{.small}

## B14: Running example {#b14 .bk}

::: {.bigtable .kv}
| quantity | value |
|---|---|
| rotor radius, air density | 63 m, 1.225 kg/m³ |
| optimum | $\lambda^\star = 7.48$, $C_P^{\mathrm{max}} = 0.4895$ |
| optimal gain | ${u^\star = 2.23\times10^6}$ N m s², normalized ${\nu^\star = 0.061}$ |
| curvature | $\chi = 6.3$, $|J''(u^\star)|u^{\star2} = 0.70$ |
| rotor time constant | 6.88 s at 8 m/s |
| dither periods | 60 s (recommended), 150 s (2019 design), 314 s (2022 tunings) |
| tracking time | one day (designs); 740 s for the design matched to the 2022 LP-ESC |
:::

## B15: A wrong design curvature {#b15 .bk}

Tuned with ${J''_\mathrm{d} = rJ''}$, the loop tracks in ${r\tau_c}$, stays unbiased, and has
amplitude ${a_\mathrm{opt}r^{-1/2}}$. The loss of Link 5 becomes

::: eqbox
$$\ell = \frac{\ell_\mathrm{min}}{2}\Big(1 + \frac1r\Big) = \frac{\sqrt r + 1/\sqrt r}{2}\cdot\frac{\ell_\mathrm{min}}{\sqrt r},$$
:::

where $\ell_\mathrm{min}/\sqrt r$ is the least loss at the tracking time $r\tau_c$ the loop actually has.

::: kv
| LP-ESC, $T$ = 60 s (Kaimal) | tracking time | $a/u^\star$ | lost, days 2–6 | predicted |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| tuned with $J''/2$ ($r = \tfrac12$) | 0.5 day | 0.133 | 0.328 % | 0.31 % |
| correct design for 0.5 day | 0.5 day | 0.112 | 0.311 % | 0.29 % |
| proposed design ($r = 1$) | 1 day | 0.094 | 0.227 % | 0.21 % |
| correct design for 2 days | 2 days | 0.079 | 0.160 % | 0.15 % |
| tuned with $2J''$ ($r = 2$) | 2 days | 0.067 | 0.172 % | 0.15 % |
:::

::: claim
Against the correct design for the same tracking time: **+5 %** ($r = \tfrac12$) and **+8 %**
($r = 2$), predicted +6 %; von Kármán gives the same. The error shows in the tracking time,
not in the energy. Mean of four six-day records; same winds as the energy table.
:::
